Alberta is the most informative row. It is the one province that finds these deaths by linking its waiting list to dates of death, and it counts people, not bookings. Its rate is the general-population rate at age 67, the same age as in BC.
The low rates need a caution. New Brunswick’s is the rate of the general population at age 54, and that more likely means its registry misses deaths than that its patients are that young.

title: What does a count of 29,000 waiting-list deaths tell us?
section: Where ages are known, fewer deaths were recorded than age alone predicts
text:
Where ages are known, fewer deaths were recorded than age alone predicts
Knee replacement is the one list for which I have real ages, because CIHI publishes them [7]. Given those ages, the BC life table predicts 131 to 150 deaths in a year among the people waiting for a knee replacement in four BC health authorities. Those authorities recorded 56.
Two things could produce that gap, and the counts cannot separate them. People accepted for a knee replacement are healthier than others of their age. Booking offices also do not learn of every death. The result holds unless the people waiting are nine to ten years younger than the people who had the operation.
For surgery as a whole I had to assume the ages, and the comparison is sensitive to what I assume, so I put little weight on it.

title: What does a count of 29,000 waiting-list deaths tell us?
section: The provinces are not counting the same thing
text:
The provinces are not counting the same thing
The recorded rates in the table differ nearly fourfold. The responses show why they would.
Cataract surgery. Patients waiting for cataract surgery are 63% of New Brunswick’s count and 26% to 37% of the count in six other provinces. Manitoba’s main response has no cataract cases at all.



Share of surgical-list deaths in 2025-26 that were on cataract lists, among the deaths that could be classified by procedure. Quebec’s share rests on the 22% of its cases that name a procedure.


One number in Quebec. Half of Quebec’s surgical total, 967 of 1,879, is a single figure from the Laurentides region for “surgical intervention or medical act.” Set against that region’s surgical list, it would be 11 deaths per 100 person-years, the rate at which the general population dies at age 88.
Scans ordered near the end of life. Ontario released 9,085 CT and MRI bookings that were cancelled because the patient died. Among the 754 with a two-day target, 46% were cancelled within a day of the order. Those are urgent scans, most likely for very sick patients, and they are in the count beside people who waited for months. Most of the Ontario bookings did wait: 82% had been open longer than their target when they were cancelled.

title: What does a count of 29,000 waiting-list deaths tell us?
section: The 17.5% rise comes from one health region
text:
The 17.5% rise comes from one health region
SecondStreet’s brief says that, among health bodies that provided data in both years, surgical waitlist deaths rose 17.5% [1]. The figure can be reproduced from the tables in its 2025 and 2026 briefs [1, 4]. Twenty-two health bodies have a surgical count in both tables, with 4,300 cases in 2024-25 and 5,053 in 2025-26.

The region’s figure for 2024-25 gives 1.3 deaths per 100 person-years, in line with other regions of Quebec. Its surgical list was 15% smaller in the second year. A sevenfold rise in deaths on a shrinking list is not credible as a change in mortality. The likelier explanation is that the two responses cover different sets of patients, and only the health body can confirm that.
The other bodies do not share a trend either. Across the 22, counts rose in 10 and fell in 12. Ontario Health says of its own imaging count that the change from year to year is driven mainly by how hospitals record cancelled entries. title: What does a count of 29,000 waiting-list deaths tell us?
text:
What this does not show
None of this shows that waiting is harmless. The counts cannot say how many of these deaths the wait caused, and that is true in both directions. Some registries appear to miss deaths, so the number of people who died while waiting could be higher than recorded. A study of Ontario patients waiting for bypass surgery found that they died at about three times the rate of the general population of the same age [8]. That study could say so because it had each patient’s age and time on the list.
SecondStreet’s brief makes a related point: no government analysed how many of these cases involved a delay that contributed to the death [1]. It cites the one review I know of, by Nova Scotia for 2022-23, in which 50 of 532 waiting-list deaths involved procedures where delay might reasonably have played a part.
My own estimate of the ages, from a model that weights each waiting list by life-table mortality, is that 60% to 74% of the surgical-list deaths were of people aged 75 and over. It rests largely on assumed ages and is the least secure result in the report.
I take no position here on how health care should be delivered or paid for. The argument is about what one count can show.

title: What does a count of 29,000 waiting-list deaths tell us?
text:
What would settle it
A province can answer the question with one table: the number of people who died while on a surgical or imaging list, by age group, procedure, and priority, found by linking the list to death registrations, and set beside the number expected from the life table. Alberta already does the linkage.
On November 25 I asked the five BC regional health authorities for their counts by age group. I will write again when the answers arrive.
SecondStreet posted every response it received, and that is what made this check possible. If you find an error in the report, please tell me.

title: Reading at 15 fell twice, and the second fall was different
text:
In an earlier post I looked at the provincial figures behind the claim that one in three 9-year-old Canadians cannot read, and I said I would write again about the international tests. This post does that. It uses the public student files from PISA, the OECD’s assessment of 15-year-olds, for 2018, 2022, and 2025 [1], and the PIRLS Grade 4 files for 2016 and 2021 [3].
My estimates reproduce the published ones. For Canada in 2022 I obtain a reading mean of 507 with a standard error of 2.0, and for Alberta on PIRLS 2021 a mean of 539 with a standard error of 3.6. Both match the official reports [2, 3].

The mean fell 13 points from 2018 to 2022 and a further 17 points from 2022 to 2025. Both changes are several times their standard errors, with the link error between cycles included.
The 2022 result was widely read as the cost of the pandemic. If school closures were the whole story, the three years after 2022 should show a pause or a partial recovery. They show a second drop at least as large as the first.

title: Reading at 15 fell twice, and the second fall was different
section: The two drops are not the same
text:
The two drops are not the same



Change in Canada’s PISA reading score at five points of the distribution. The 10th percentile is the score below which the weakest tenth of students fall.


From 2018 to 2022, the weakest readers lost the most. The score at the 10th percentile fell 22 points, and the score at the 90th percentile fell 3, a change that is within sampling error. That pattern is what an interruption of schooling would produce if stronger students were better able to keep learning without it.
From 2022 to 2025, the loss was about the same everywhere: 15 to 21 points at every percentile I examined. Strong readers, who had held their ground through the pandemic years, fell as far as weak ones.
I do not know what caused the second drop. The data rule out some explanations, which I take up below, and they do not identify one.

title: Reading at 15 fell twice, and the second fall was different
section: The provinces fell at different times
text:
The provinces fell at different times



PISA reading means by province, from CMEC’s published table. Standard errors range from about 3 points in the larger provinces to about 10 in Prince Edward Island.


Every province scored lower in 2025 than in 2018 [2]. The timing differs.

Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, and Saskatchewan took most of their decline by 2022 and changed little afterward.
Alberta, British Columbia, and Prince Edward Island changed little by 2022 and fell afterward. Alberta fell 26 points between 2022 and 2025.
Quebec, Ontario, and New Brunswick fell in both periods. Manitoba fell by 8 and 9 points, the smallest total decline along with Saskatchewan’s.

The provincial figures for 2025 are CMEC’s. The public file for 2025 does not identify provinces within Canada, so I could not recompute them.

title: Reading at 15 fell twice, and the second fall was different
section: Three explanations the data do not support
text:
Three explanations the data do not support
A change in who is in the classroom. I reweighted the 2025 sample so that the shares of non-immigrant, second-generation, and first-generation students match those of 2018. The 2025 mean moves from 490 to 492. Immigration does not explain a 30-point decline.
A change in who wrote the test. About 77% of sampled students took part in both 2022 and 2025, and Statistics Canada found that the students who took part had higher school marks than those who did not [2]. That biases each year’s score upward. It biases the change only if the bias itself changed. For the 17-point drop to be an artefact, the gap between participants and non-participants would have had to shrink by about 75 points in three years, with participation unchanged. The OECD’s own review reached the same view and called the effect on the 2022 to 2025 comparison negligible [2].
The pandemic alone. The cohort tested in 2025 was in Grade 4 or 5 when schools closed in 2020, so lasting harm from the closures is possible. A closure effect, however, would be expected to look like the first drop and fall hardest on weak readers. The second drop does not look like that.

title: Reading at 15 fell twice, and the second fall was different
section: In Grade 4, where a comparison exists, there is no drop
text:
In Grade 4, where a comparison exists, there is no drop
Quebec is the only province with its own PIRLS sample in both 2016 and 2021. Its Grade 4 mean was 547 in 2016 and 551 in 2021, a difference within sampling error. The share of students below the Low benchmark was 1.6% and 1.2%.
In 2021, the share below the Low benchmark was 5.0% in Alberta, 5.7% in British Columbia, and 7.5% in Newfoundland and Labrador. The share below the Intermediate benchmark, which is the figure the Aristotle Foundation report used for Alberta [4], was 20%, 21%, and 26%.
One province and one pair of years is thin evidence. It is still worth setting beside the 15-year-old results: the largest measured declines are in adolescence, and the public debate is about how reading is taught in Grades 1 to 3.

title: Reading at 15 fell twice, and the second fall was different
text:
What this does not show
It does not show why scores fell after 2022. The candidates people raise, among them phones, attendance, and the long tail of the closures, are not tested here.
It does not show that the 2025 numbers are exact. Canada did not meet the PISA standard for student participation in 2022 or 2025, and seven provinces carry a caution flag in 2025 [2]. The levels are probably somewhat too high in both years. The change between them is on firmer ground than either level.
It does not bear on the early-reading reforms. A student who started Grade 1 under Alberta’s new curriculum in 2022 will be 15 in about 2031.

title: Reading at 15 fell twice, and the second fall was different
text:
What would settle it
The 2025 public file has no province codes for Canada. With them, the percentile analysis above could be done province by province, and one could see whether Alberta’s late drop looks like Newfoundland’s early one. CMEC holds those codes.
PIRLS 2026 was written last spring. Its results, due in December 2027, will give Grade 4 figures that can be set against 2021 for more provinces than Quebec.
The R scripts behind these numbers are available on request. If you find an error, please tell me.

title: Your leaderboard gap is probably noise
text: Somewhere right now, a team is choosing which AI model to build on because it sits one place higher on a leaderboard. The gap might be two points of win rate, or a handful of Elo. Here’s the uncomfortable question a statistician has to ask: is that gap a fact about the models, or a fact about the sample?

title: Your leaderboard gap is probably noise
text:
A two-minute calculation
Suppose model A beats model B in 62% of head-to-head comparisons, and model B wins 60% of its own matchups, each measured over 500 votes. Two points apart — feels decisive on a ranking table.
The standard error of a proportion around 0.6 on 500 votes is \(\sqrt{0.6 \times 0.4 / 500} \approx 0.022\) — about 2.2 percentage points per model. The uncertainty on the difference between them is larger still, roughly \(\sqrt{2} \times 2.2 \approx 3.1\) points. A 2-point observed gap against ~3 points of noise, before any multiple-comparison correction, isn’t evidence of a real difference. It’s a tie wearing a trophy.
This isn’t a contrived example. Public arena leaderboards now publish confidence intervals precisely because the intervals at the top routinely overlap — the rank order among the leading models is partly an artifact of sampling. And the problem compounds: with ten models, there are forty-five pairwise comparisons, so a few “significant-looking” gaps will appear by chance even if nothing real separates anyone.

title: Your leaderboard gap is probably noise
section: The deeper problem: rankings are measurements
text:
The deeper problem: rankings are measurements
A leaderboard is a measurement instrument, and instruments have reliability. The question that matters isn’t only “is this gap significant today?” but “if we collected the same number of votes again, would the ranking come back the same?” Those are different questions. A gap can clear a significance test while the ranking built from many such gaps remains unstable — flip a few hundred votes and third place becomes sixth.
Measurement theory has a name for this and a toolbox for it: you decompose the variation in observed scores into the part that reflects real differences between the things being ranked and the part that’s occasion-to-occasion noise, then compute how many observations you’d need before the ranking is dependable at the level you care about. The recurring finding, in domain after domain, is that the number is larger than people expect — often much larger than the data anyone has.

title: Your leaderboard gap is probably noise
section: How to read a leaderboard without fooling yourself
text:
How to read a leaderboard without fooling yourself
Ask for the interval, not the point: if the intervals of two entries overlap, treat them as tied, whatever the rank order says. Ask for the n behind each comparison — a rating built on 80 matchups and one built on 8,000 do not deserve the same trust. Be most suspicious exactly where the stakes feel highest, at the top, where entries are closest and gaps are smallest relative to noise. And if a decision genuinely hangs on the comparison — which model to license, which system to ship — run your own evaluation on your own task distribution, sized in advance so the answer will be reliable. That last step is a sample-size calculation, and it’s cheaper than choosing the wrong model.
None of this is exotic statistics. It’s the same discipline clinical trials have used for decades, pointed at a new kind of scoreboard. The scoreboards are new; the arithmetic isn’t.
I consult on exactly these questions — evaluation design, the reliability of ranking and judging pipelines, and how much data a trustworthy verdict needs. If your team is making decisions off a leaderboard, let’s talk.

title: For health researchers and clinical teams
text: Health studies are expensive to run and hard to repeat, so the design has to be right the first time. I help clinical and health-services teams plan studies that can answer their question, and analyze them in a way that claims no more than the data support.

title: For health researchers and clinical teams
text:
What people usually ask me

How many participants do we need, allowing for dropout and clustering?
Our outcome is measured repeatedly. How should we model it?
How reliable is our rating scale or our raters?
Can our design support a comparison between subgroups, such as by sex?
What will the journal’s reporting guideline expect from our statistics section?


How I help

title: For health researchers and clinical teams
text:
What the work looks like

Design: sample size and power, randomization, and a statistical analysis plan for the protocol or ethics application.
Analysis: mixed-effects and generalized linear models for repeated, clustered, and count outcomes.
Measurement: reliability of instruments, raters, and scores, including how many ratings or occasions a dependable score needs.
Data handling: de-identified data wherever possible, and work within your ethics board’s conditions. See confidentiality and data handling.
Reporting: methods and results written for clinicians and reviewers, with limitations stated in numbers.

title: For engineering and manufacturing teams
text: Every experimental run costs something: machine time, material, or a day of production. Design of experiments is how you make each run answer several questions at once. It is my main research area.

title: For engineering and manufacturing teams
text:

We have ten factors that might matter. How do we find the few that do?

How I help

title: For engineering and manufacturing teams
text:
What the work looks like

Screening: fractional-factorial designs that sort the important factors from the rest in few runs.
Optimization: follow-up designs to find the best settings for the factors that matter.
Designs with a baseline: when each factor has a default level, designs under the baseline parameterization estimate effects relative to that default directly. Most of my published papers are on these designs.
Testing: covering arrays and related designs for testing systems with many settings.
Training: design of experiments workshops for engineers, built around your own processes where possible.
